pieces.title: Let’s Be Demanding of Government, but Not Cheaply Cynical About It
pieces.author: Vishaan Chakrabarti
pieces.dek: Connecting the dots between the midterms and better scaffolding=

posts.text: Vishaan Chakrabarti argues that cynicism about government is a vicious circle: the more we pile on petty critiques of every shortfall, the slower and more imperfect public work becomes.
Read Vishaan Chakrabarti, an architect who works mostly for government, on the mock-up sidewalk sheds at Broadway and Chambers Street and the online snark that greeted them.
"People see the widespread failures brought on by our collective shortsightedness, and then become jaded when we try to fix any of it." Vishaan Chakrabarti on cynicism and the midterms.

pieces.title: The Midterms Taught New York a Lesson About Character
pieces.author: Nicole Gelinas
pieces.dek: Like or loathe their policies, Hochul and Mamdani tend to behave like decent human beings. Blakeman, not so much.

posts.text: Nicole Gelinas argues Bruce Blakeman lost in part on character: he twice tried to use 9/11 for political points, and voters who paid attention noticed. Policy ideas were only part of it.
Read @nicolegelinas on why New York Republicans cannot beat Zohran Mamdani by attacking him as a person, and what Kathy Hochul and Mamdani did at the 9/11 ceremonies that Bruce Blakeman did not.
"Politicians are not just collections of platform planks; they are people." Nicole Gelinas on what the midterms showed about Bruce Blakeman, Hochul and Mamdani.

pieces.title: The Fiscal Significance of Mamdani’s Union Contracts
pieces.author: Tal Roded
pieces.dek: The agreements City Hall inks with organized labor will largely determine the magnitude of future budget gaps.

posts.text: Tal Roded argues that Mayor Mamdani should tie any pay raises for municipal unions to work rule reforms, because 3% annual raises would add billions to budget gaps that already exist.
Read Tal Roded on the DC 37 contract and what it means for the city budget. Roded says it will set the pattern for every other union, and Mayor Mamdani has to bargain hard.
How much does a 3% raise cost New York City? Tal Roded puts it at roughly $4 billion a year by year four, above what the budget plans for, on top of a $7.3 billion gap in fiscal year 2028.

pieces.title: There’s No Tenable Way To Integrate New York’s Schools from the Top Down
pieces.author: Tim DeRoche
pieces.dek: A tough truth that Zohran Mamdani and Nikole Hannah-Jones must reckon with

posts.text: Tim DeRoche argues that every route to forced integration of New York City schools is illegal, unpopular or both. The one option he sees left is to end zoned student assignment, as New Orleans did.
Read Tim DeRoche on why Mayor Mamdani can't integrate the city's schools from the top down, and what DeRoche says he could do instead about the zone map dividing P.S. 307 from the Roebling School.

Why can't children zoned to P.S. 307 attend the Roebling School less than a mile away? Tim DeRoche says it's an attendance zone line drawn and enforced by the Department of Education, and school choice has little to do with it.

pieces.title: It Wasn’t the Dutch Who Shaped New Amsterdam
pieces.author: Alan Mikhail
pieces.dek: A close reading of the letter that recorded the purchase of Manhattan from Native peoples

posts.text: The Schagen Letter is famous for the 60 guilders. Alan Mikhail argues its most important detail is a passing line about women giving birth to "some children," a sign that the colony might last.
Read Alan Mikhail on who actually built New Amsterdam: Catalina Trico, Anthony the Turk, Mayken van Angola and others who stayed for decades, long after the fur traders left.

Who were the real founders of the colony that became New York? Alan Mikhail says the people who stayed longest: "the enslaved, the rejected, the religiously othered, the hustlers, the rabble-rousers."

pieces.title: What Does Zohran Mamdani’s Office of Mass Engagement Really Do?
pieces.author: Sage Lattman
pieces.dek: A view from the pavement

posts.text: Sage Lattman went canvassing with Mayor Mamdani's Office of Mass Engagement and finds the events stay within the law. Whether they actually protect tenants, Lattman says, is unclear. The volunteers, though, are inspired.

Read @sagelattman on what Organize New York City does on the ground. Lattman attended two Talk to Tenants canvasses and a tenant organizing session, and asked a Columbia law professor whether any of it crosses a line.

"Government doesn't have to always be impartial if they think there's one side that needs help," says Columbia law professor Richard Briffault, on the Mamdani administration's tenant organizing, in Sage Lattman's reporting.

pieces.title: Did Federal Local Fiscal Recovery Funding Drive America’s Postpandemic Homicide Decline?
pieces.author: Ethan Doshi
pieces.dek: A close look at the evidence says it doesn't look likely.

posts.text: Cities that got more federal recovery money than similar cities in their state saw no bigger drop in homicide, finds Ethan Doshi. The biggest surges, he writes, produced the biggest declines.
Read Ethan Doshi on whether American Rescue Plan money drove the postpandemic homicide decline. He tested the theory across hundreds of cities and says the signal isn't there.
Why did homicide fall fastest in the cities that got the most federal money? Ethan Doshi says the formula sent money to the hardest-hit places, and those places were already due to fall back.

pieces.title: Taking Gun Violence Seriously
pieces.author: Philip J. Cook
pieces.dek: On Malcolm Gladwell's latest book, "The American Way of Killing"

posts.text: Philip J. Cook says Malcolm Gladwell is right that American police forces are too small, but wrong that trauma care explains the homicide numbers. Chicago shooting data shows why.
Read Philip J. Cook, who has researched American gun violence for 50 years, on Malcolm Gladwell's "The American Way of Killing": what the book gets right, and where he says it misses.
Did better trauma care keep the homicide rate from tripling? Philip J. Cook checked Gladwell's claim against Chicago shooting data and the National Crime Victimization Survey.

pieces.title: How Unchecked Immigration Enforcement Risks Making U.S. Cities Less Safe
pieces.author: Nayna Gupta
pieces.dek: ICE actions are harming trust between locals and police.

posts.text: Nayna Gupta argues that no amount of effective local policing can make up for what aggressive federal immigration enforcement does to public trust in police, and so to public safety.
Read Nayna Gupta on what happens when local police become a force multiplier for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and what New York City and other cities can do about it.

Does involving local police in immigration enforcement make cities safer? Nayna Gupta points to a new American Economic Review study: Hispanic victims reported fewer crimes and were more likely to become victims.

pieces.title: When ICE Comes to Town: The Role of Law, Local Police and Neighbors
pieces.author: Vital City
pieces.dek: Former Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson, immigration researcher Austin Kocher and Documented reporter Eileen Grench on what police should do when an immigration operation comes to a city.

posts.text: Former Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson says local police should keep a role when federal agents work their neighborhoods. Refusing to cooperate with ICE, he argues, is counterproductive for public safety.

Read researcher Austin Kocher on who ICE is arresting. He says all the growth in arrests since last summer came from people with no criminal charges or convictions, a gap he says the data shows against the rhetoric.

"When you're out on the streets, use your common sense." Jeh Johnson says he told ICE that as Homeland Security Secretary. Hear him, Austin Kocher and Eileen Grench on what police should do when ICE comes to a city.

pieces.title: Daniel Penny and Jordan Neely, Through Cracked Looking Glass
pieces.author: Brandon del Pozo
pieces.dek: What to make of "Man in the Mirror," Anand Giridharadas' impressive but incomplete new book

posts.text: Brandon del Pozo says Anand Giridharadas' book on Jordan Neely and Daniel Penny gets the failed mental health system right and the Penny trial wrong, treating an acquittal as justice denied.

Read @brandondelpozo, a former New York City Police Department precinct commander, on "Man in the Mirror." He finds it important but incomplete, and says it never considers what the killing did to Penny as a person.
"To bristle at the proceedings of a criminal trial because it isn't a fulsome portrait of anyone involved is to fundamentally misunderstand its purpose," writes Brandon del Pozo on the Penny trial.

pieces.title: The Other Time New York Bled Orange and Blue
pieces.author: Jere Hester
pieces.dek: 40 years ago, the Mets did the impossible — and brought the city together.

posts.text: Jere Hester was in the Shea Stadium stands for Game 6 in 1986 and on the streets for the Knicks title this June. He writes that both wins briefly united a fractured city.
Read Jere Hester on the Mets in 1986, the Knicks this year, and what two championships 40 years apart did for New York City. He was at Shea Stadium for the first and in the streets for the second.
"The Mets made us a family." Mayor Ed Koch said it in 1986. Jere Hester writes that Mayor Zohran Mamdani echoed him at the Knicks parade, and that New York City got the magic twice in one lifetime.

pieces.title: Let’s Be Honest. LinkNYC Has Been a Failure.
pieces.author: Michael Samuelian
pieces.dek: Why the de Blasio-era experiment was the wrong model and what we should do about it

posts.text: Michael Samuelian argues LinkNYC failed because the City built a public utility on a private advertiser's balance sheet, then looked away. The 32-foot Link5G towers, he says, repeat the mistake.
Read Michael Samuelian on LinkNYC at ten. He lays out four structural failures, from backward geography to absent oversight, and proposes a public Broadband Development Corporation instead.
"New York doesn't need taller 5G towers. It needs a landlord who owns the pipes." Michael Samuelian on what the City should do after ten years of LinkNYC.

pieces.title: Money and Politics in New York City: A Frontline Perspective
pieces.author: Maya Kornberg
pieces.dek: A former candidate for the New York City Council explains the complications of campaign financing.

posts.text: Maya Kornberg ran for the New York City Council with public matching funds. She says outside groups spent over $400,000 backing her, and many voters blamed her campaign for the ads anyway.
Read Maya Kornberg, a political scientist and former City Council candidate, on what outside spending did to her race and why she wants Citizens United overturned.
"I was no longer in control of how voters experienced messaging about my goals or values." Maya Kornberg on running for City Council amid outside spending.

pieces.title: Letitia James on Donald Trump, Defending State Law and Her Case for Reelection as New York Attorney General
pieces.author: New York Editorial Board
pieces.dek: The New York Editorial Board's interview with New York Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat seeking reelection in 2026.

posts.text: Letitia James tells the New York Editorial Board that criminal enforcement is maybe a quarter of her office's work, and that public safety is mainly a matter for district attorneys and the police commissioner.

Read the New York Editorial Board's interview with Attorney General Letitia James on Donald Trump, subway crime, Atlantic Yards and police killings. Nicole Gelinas, Alyssa Katz and Ben Smith are among the questioners.

"I'm not fighting Donald Trump. What I'm doing is protecting the rights of New Yorkers." Letitia James, in an interview with the New York Editorial Board, on her case for a third term as attorney general.

pieces.title: Saritha Komatireddy on Public Safety, Law Enforcement and Her Campaign for New York Attorney General
pieces.author: New York Editorial Board
pieces.dek: The New York Editorial Board's interview with Saritha Komatireddy, the Republican nominee for New York attorney general in the 2026 election.

posts.text: Saritha Komatireddy, the Republican nominee for attorney general, says she would move 350 of the office's 700 assistant attorneys general onto criminal prosecution. She told the New York Editorial Board how.

The New York Editorial Board sat down with Saritha Komatireddy, a former federal prosecutor running for attorney general, and pressed her on crime data, Alvin Bragg and the Justice Department under Trump.

What can an attorney general do when a district attorney charges too low? Saritha Komatireddy tells the New York Editorial Board she would use Executive Law 63 to take the case over and prosecute it herself.

pieces.title: New York’s Devilish Assault Problem
pieces.author: Vital City, Paul Reeping
pieces.dek: What's driving it and what's next?

posts.text: Paul Reeping tested the usual explanations for New York City's rise in assaults, from hotspots to repeat offenders to subway crime. Most contribute. None drives it. The rise is citywide and mostly among people who know each other.
Read @paulreeping on why assaults keep rising in New York City while murders and shootings fall. His answer starts with the city doing deeper analysis of the detailed data it already holds.

Why are assaults up 20% since 2019 in New York City when they are falling nationally? Paul Reeping checks six common explanations against the data. Stranger attacks, hotspots and the subway are part of it, none the main cause.

pieces.title: From San Juan Hill to Lincoln Center and Back
pieces.author: Julia Foulkes
pieces.dek: How cultural institutions should respect what they displace

posts.text: Julia Foulkes argues that Lincoln Center's San Juan Hill festival is a long-overdue attempt to make a cultural treasure welcome to a wider range of New Yorkers, and that its new design should open outward too.
Read Julia Foulkes on what Lincoln Center replaced. San Juan Hill gave New York City stride piano, "Shuffle Along" and the Charleston before it was cleared for the performing arts complex.
"It can be an elite cultural treasure — but it need not and should not be only for elites." Julia Foulkes on Lincoln Center, San Juan Hill and what an institution owes the neighborhood it displaced.

pieces.title: How ICE Puts the NYPD in an Impossible Position
pieces.author: John Hall
pieces.dek: Those pointing fingers at the police department in the wake of the Marble Hill shooting fail to understand its legal constraints and responsibilities.

posts.text: John Hall argues the New York City Police Department has little choice in how it responds to ICE: city law bars it from assisting civil immigration enforcement, and federal law bars it from obstructing federal agents.

Read John Hall on the Marble Hill shooting and the police department's legal position. Hall says City Hall should issue clear public guidelines on what officers may and may not do when ICE is on the street.
"The feds cause a mess, and local police take much of the blame." John Hall on what Newark's Delaney Hall protests show about where New York City is heading.

pieces.title: Make the Governor Responsible for New York’s Schools
pieces.author: Daniel Weisberg
pieces.dek: Learn from mayoral control, and from other states

posts.text: Daniel Weisberg argues New York's governor should pick the Board of Regents, which would then pick the education commissioner. A change in state law would do it, he says. No constitutional amendment needed.
Read Daniel Weisberg on what New York could learn from mayoral control and from Mississippi, Tennessee and Louisiana about who should be answerable for the state's schools.
Who is in charge of New York's schools? Daniel Weisberg says the governor has no say over the Regents or the commissioner, and that the "maybes" mean no one is in charge.
